name: Sunk Cost Fallacy
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Throwing Good Money After Qubits
lesson.summary: The sunk cost fallacy, continuing to invest because of what has already been spent rather than what is likely to pay off going forward, is a well documented cognitive bias that helps explain the institutional momentum behind large quantum computing programs regardless of updated evidence.
lesson.body:
Rational decision making, in theory, only weighs costs and benefits that lie ahead of the decision being made. Money, time, or effort already spent is gone no matter what choice comes next, so it should have no bearing on whether continuing is the right call. In practice, people and institutions routinely violate this principle, continuing to pour resources into a project specifically because they have already invested heavily in it, a pattern well documented across psychology and behavioral economics and known as the sunk cost fallacy.

One of the clearest historical illustrations is the Concorde supersonic passenger jet, a joint program between the British and French governments that continued for years even as it became increasingly clear the economics would never work out, the plane was expensive to operate, limited in range, and never came close to recovering its enormous development costs. The pattern is well documented enough that behavioral researchers sometimes refer to this specific dynamic as the Concorde fallacy: having already committed enormous public sums, walking away felt like admitting the money was wasted, which made continuing psychologically and politically easier than stopping, even as the forward-looking case for stopping grew stronger.

The parallel to quantum computing is not subtle. Governments and large technology companies have committed substantial sums, in some cases spanning two decades of sustained investment, to quantum computing research programs. Once an organization has a dedicated quantum computing division, a public roadmap with specific milestones, and a leadership team whose professional reputation is tied to the program's eventual success, the institutional incentives tilt heavily toward continuing and publicly defending the investment rather than recalibrating in response to new evidence. Admitting a multi-year, multi-billion-dollar program might not pay off as promised carries real reputational and political costs that have nothing to do with the technology's actual prospects.

It is important to be precise about what this argument does and does not establish. Pointing out sunk cost reasoning does not by itself prove that current quantum computing investment is a mistake, the underlying technology might still turn out to be valuable within its narrow applicable domain, discussed in earlier chapters. The point is narrower and more logical than that: "we have already spent so much, we cannot stop now" is never, on its own, a valid argument for continuing an investment. Only the expected value of the next dollar spent, weighed against alternatives, is a valid argument, and that calculation is completely independent of how much has already been spent.

This bias rarely operates in isolation. It tends to interact with, and reinforce, other biases covered elsewhere in this book, particularly optimism bias about how close a payoff really is and bandwagon dynamics that make continued investment feel validated by the fact that others are investing too. How these individual biases compound into something larger than any one of them is the subject of a later chapter.
